pages.question: A 55-year-old Asian female presents to the clinic with sudden onset chest discomfort and shortness of breath. She recently concluded a 14-hour flight and has a history of mild hypertension controlled with diet. Vital signs reveal a blood pressure of 120/80 mmHg and a pulse rate of 100 beats per minute. On examination, she appears anxious, and oxygen saturation is recorded at 94% on room air. A chest X-ray is unremarkable, and upon performing an ECG, sinus tachycardia is noted. To further investigate, a ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) scan is performed. Which finding below is most consistent with your primary suspicion?

answers.text: Uniform clearance of both ventilation and perfusion scans.
Multiple small ventilation and perfusion defects.
A large area of perfusion defect without ventilation defect.
A large area of ventilation defect without a perfusion defect.

pages.question: A 55-year-old Asian female presents to the clinic with sudden onset chest discomfort and shortness of breath. She recently concluded a 14-hour flight and has a history of mild hypertension controlled with diet. Vital signs reveal a blood pressure of 120/80 mmHg and a pulse rate of 100 beats per minute. On examination, she appears anxious, and oxygen saturation is recorded at 94% on room air. A chest X-ray is unremarkable, and upon performing an ECG, sinus tachycardia is noted. To further investigate, a ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) scan is performed. Which finding below is most consistent with your primary suspicion?

answers.text:
Uniform clearance of both ventilation and perfusion scans.
(0%)

Multiple small ventilation and perfusion defects.
(1.33%)

A large area of perfusion defect without ventilation defect.
(84.67%)

A large area of ventilation defect without a perfusion defect.
(11.33%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
The clinical scenario of sudden onset chest discomfort and shortness of breath following prolonged immobility (14-hour flight) in a patient with risk factors strongly suggests pulmonary embolism. A V/Q scan showing a large perfusion defect without ventilation defect (mismatched defect) is the classic finding for PE, representing areas where blood flow is blocked by emboli but ventilation remains normal. This high-probability pattern, when combined with appropriate clinical context, supports the diagnosis of pulmonary embolism.
(Choice A)
Matched ventilation and perfusion defects.
Matched ventilation and perfusion defects occur when both airflow and blood flow are reduced in the same lung region, typically due to pneumonia, atelectasis, or chronic lung disease. Unlike pulmonary embolism, the ventilation and perfusion abnormalities correspond to each other.
(Choice B)
Uniform clearance of both ventilation and perfusion scans.
Normal ventilation and perfusion patterns throughout both lungs indicate no areas of impaired blood flow or air exchange, effectively ruling out pulmonary embolism. This would be interpreted as a 'normal' V/Q scan.
(Choice C)
Multiple small ventilation and perfusion defects.
Multiple small ventilation and perfusion defects are nonspecific and typically classified as 'low probability' for pulmonary embolism on V/Q scan interpretation. This pattern is inconclusive and requires further evaluation with CT pulmonary angiogram (CTPA) or other imaging modalities.
(Choice D)
A large area of perfusion defect without ventilation defect.
In persons with suspected pulmonary embolism, a large perfusion defect with no ventilation defect is highly indicative of the condition and termed a 'mismatched defect'.
(Choice E)
A large area of ventilation defect without a perfusion defect.
A ventilation defect without perfusion defect suggests airway obstruction or parenchymal lung disease (such as pneumonia or COPD exacerbation) where air cannot reach the alveoli but blood flow remains intact. This pattern is opposite to what occurs in pulmonary embolism.

pages.question:
A 35-year-old female elementary school teacher presents with recurrent episodes of severe, sharp pain in the rectal area that last for about 5-10 minutes and resolve spontaneously. She reports that these episodes often occur during periods of high stress, such as parent-teacher conferences, and are not associated with bowel movements, sexual activity, or changes in position. She has experienced approximately 2-3 episodes per month for the past year. Physical examination, including digital rectal exam, pelvic exam, and anoscopy, is normal. Laboratory test are shown below. Colonoscopy performed 6 months ago for routine screening was normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?



Hemoglobin	13.6 g/dL
Hematocrit	41%
Red blood cell count	4.8 x10^6/µL
Mean corpuscular volume	88 fL
Mean corpuscular hemoglobin	30 pg
Mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration	34 g/dL
Red cell distribution width	12.5%
White blood cell count	7200/µL
Neutrophils	60%
Lymphocytes	30%
Monocytes	6%
Eosinophils	3%
Basophils	1%
Platelet count	260000/µL
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate	10 mm/hr
C-reactive protein	0.6 mg/L
pages.explanation:
Explanation
This patient has recurrent, brief episodes of rectal pain triggered by stress, unrelated to defecation or other activities, with normal physical examination and laboratory findings, consistent with proctalgia fugax.
(Choice A)
Internal hemorrhoids
Internal hemorrhoids usually present with painless bleeding or prolapse, not episodic sharp pain without defecation association, and would likely be visible on anoscopy or colonoscopy, both normal in this case.
(Choice B)
Levator ani syndrome
Levator ani syndrome involves chronic or recurrent deep pelvic/rectal pain lasting 20 minutes to several hours, often with tenderness on palpation of the levator muscles during digital rectal exam. This differs from the brief 5-10 minute episodes with normal physical examination findings in this patient.
(Choice C)
Inflammatory bowel disease
Inflammatory bowel disease typically involves diarrhea, abdominal pain, weight loss, and mucosal abnormalities on colonoscopy, which was normal here, and pain is not characteristically brief and episodic without other symptoms.
(Choice D)
Endometriosis
Endometriosis involving the rectovaginal septum can cause cyclical pelvic pain typically related to menstrual cycles, often with dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, or dyschezia. The pain pattern would be cyclical rather than stress-triggered, and pelvic examination often reveals nodularity or tenderness.
(Choice E)
Proctalgia fugax
Proctalgia fugax presents with recurrent, brief episodes of severe rectal pain that resolve spontaneously, often triggered by stress, with no abnormalities on physical exam or labs, fitting this patient's presentation as a diagnosis of exclusion.

pages.question: A 52-year-old woman who recently immigrated from Mexico presents to the clinic for management of type 2 diabetes mellitus. She speaks limited English and requires an interpreter. Her hemoglobin A1c is elevated, and the physician decides to initiate metformin therapy. To minimize the risk of medication errors during reconciliation, which of the following is the most appropriate action for the physician to take?

answers.text:
Communicate the instructions solely to the interpreter and ask them to relay the information later
(2.25%)

Ask the patient's accompanying adult daughter to translate the medication instructions
(0%)

Provide the patient with written instructions in English and ask her to review them at home
(0%)

Use a qualified interpreter and directly ask the patient to explain in her own words how she will take the metformin
(95.51%)

Prescribe the medication and schedule a follow-up visit in 2 weeks without confirming the patient's understanding of medication instructions
(2.25%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
Patients with limited English proficiency face a high risk of medication errors due to communication barriers. Effective strategies include engaging a qualified medical interpreter, speaking directly to the patient, providing translated educational materials, and using teach-back methods to confirm understanding. Relying on family members or untrained interpreters is not recommended.
(Choice A)
Communicate the instructions solely to the interpreter and ask them to relay the information later
This is incorrect because physicians must communicate directly with the patient through the interpreter, not solely with the interpreter. Direct patient-physician communication builds therapeutic rapport, ensures real-time clarification of questions, and allows the physician to assess the patient's understanding through nonverbal cues.
(Choice B)
Ask the patient's accompanying adult daughter to translate the medication instructions
This is incorrect because using family members as interpreters, even adult children, is not recommended due to potential for translation inaccuracies, emotional bias, confidentiality concerns, and the family member's lack of medical terminology knowledge. Qualified medical interpreters should be used instead.
(Choice C)
Provide the patient with written instructions in English and ask her to review them at home
This is incorrect because providing materials only in English to a patient with limited English proficiency creates a significant communication barrier, increasing the risk of misunderstanding medication instructions and subsequent medication errors.
(Choice D)
Use a qualified interpreter and directly ask the patient to explain in her own words how she will take the metformin
This is correct as it incorporates a qualified interpreter, direct communication with the patient, and the teach-back technique to confirm understanding, reducing medication errors.
(Choice E)
Prescribe the medication and schedule a follow-up visit in 2 weeks without confirming the patient's understanding of medication instructions
This is incorrect because it fails to address communication barriers and does not verify the patient's comprehension, heightening the risk of errors.

pages.question: A 45-year-old man arrives at the emergency department after being caught in a warehouse fire. His body temperature is 39.2°C (102.5°F), blood pressure is 90/55 mm Hg, heart rate is 120/min, and respiratory rate is 22/min. He has sustained third-degree burns covering 60% of his total body surface area, including facial burns with singed nasal hairs and soot in the nasal passages. During examination, he is conscious but exhibits signs of respiratory distress. His carboxyhemoglobin level reads 20%. What is the most urgent initial treatment for this patient?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
To ensure patient safety and effective treatment, early airway management, typically via intubation, is paramount in burn victims exhibiting signs of inhalation trauma. Delay can lead to obstruction as airway edema progresses, complicating further intubation efforts.
(Choice A)
Immediate debridement
While debridement of necrotic tissue is important for burn wound management and infection prevention, it is not an immediate life-threatening priority. The ABCs (airway, breathing, circulation) must be addressed first, as airway edema can rapidly progress to complete obstruction.
(Choice B)
Immediate bronchoscopy
Bronchoscopy is valuable for assessing the extent of airway injury and can guide management decisions, but it is not the immediate priority when a patient shows signs of respiratory distress and impending airway compromise. Securing the airway takes precedence over diagnostic procedures.
(Choice C)
Intravenous calcium gluconate
Calcium gluconate is specifically indicated for hydrofluoric acid burns to bind fluoride ions and prevent systemic toxicity. It has no role in managing airway compromise or carbon monoxide poisoning from thermal inhalation injury.
(Choice D)
Epinephrine nebulization
Epinephrine nebulization may provide temporary relief for upper airway edema in some inflammatory conditions, but it is inadequate for managing thermal injury to the airway. The heat damage and progressive edema require definitive airway protection through intubation.
(Choice E)
Endotracheal intubation
Correct choice. Early intubation is critical to secure the airway in burn victims, especially when there are signs of inhalation injury and progressive airway edema risk.

pages.question:
A 72-year-old woman from a rural area in sub-Saharan Africa presents with a 3-month history of increasing weakness, unintentional weight loss of 8 kg, intermittent low-grade fevers, night sweats, and a persistent nonproductive cough. She reports recent episodes of nausea, vomiting, and lightheadedness upon standing. On examination, she is cachectic with orthostatic hypotension (supine blood pressure 110/70 mmHg, standing 85/55 mmHg) and diffuse skin hyperpigmentation. Laboratory results are shown below. A chest radiograph shows diffuse small nodular opacities in a miliary pattern. Sputum acid-fast bacillus smear is positive. What is the most likely etiology of this patient's adrenal insufficiency?



White Blood Cell Count (WBC)	6.5×109/L
Red Blood Cell Count (RBC)	4.80×1012/L
Hemoglobin (Hgb)	14.2 g/dL
Hematocrit (Hct)	42.5 %
Mean Corpuscular Volume (MCV)	88.5 fL
Mean Corpuscular Hemoglobin (MCH)	29.5 pg
Platelet Count	220×109/L
Sodium	125 mEq/L
Potassium	6.1 mEq/L
Blood Urea Nitrogen (BUN)	35 mg/dL
Serum Creatinine	1.4 mg/dL
Glucose	65 mg/dL
Morning Cortisol	2.5 μg/dL	(normal: 5-25 μg/dL)
Adrenocorticotropic Hormone (ACTH)	450 pg/mL	(normal: 7-69 pg/mL)
pages.explanation:
Explanation
The patient has primary adrenal insufficiency due to miliary tuberculosis, as evidenced by constitutional symptoms, pulmonary findings consistent with miliary TB, positive AFB smear, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypoglycemia, low cortisol with elevated ACTH, and signs of aldosterone deficiency distinguishing it from secondary causes. Other etiologies do not account for the infectious and pulmonary features.
(Choice A)
Adrenal hemorrhage
Bilateral adrenal hemorrhage can cause acute primary adrenal insufficiency, typically occurring in the setting of anticoagulation, sepsis, trauma, or coagulopathy. However, this condition usually presents with acute onset of severe abdominal or flank pain and hemodynamic instability, rather than the chronic 3-month course described. The miliary pulmonary findings and positive AFB smear are inconsistent with hemorrhagic adrenal destruction.
(Choice B)
Pituitary apoplexy
Pituitary apoplexy causes secondary adrenal insufficiency due to ACTH deficiency. In secondary adrenal insufficiency, aldosterone production by the zona glomerulosa remains intact (as it is primarily regulated by the renin-angiotensin system), so patients typically do not develop the severe hyperkalemia and volume depletion seen here. Additionally, pituitary apoplexy would not explain the pulmonary miliary pattern or positive AFB smear.
(Choice C)
Autoimmune adrenalitis
Autoimmune adrenalitis (Addison's disease) is the most common cause of primary adrenal insufficiency in developed countries. However, it typically presents as an isolated endocrine disorder without systemic infectious symptoms. The presence of fever, night sweats, productive respiratory symptoms, miliary chest radiograph pattern, and positive AFB smear strongly suggests an infectious etiology rather than autoimmune destruction of the adrenal glands.
(Choice D)
Infectious adrenalitis
Infectious adrenalitis due to miliary tuberculosis explains the patient's primary adrenal insufficiency with aldosterone deficiency (hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypovolemia), constitutional symptoms, pulmonary miliary pattern, and positive AFB smear, consistent with disseminated TB affecting the adrenal glands.
(Choice E)
Metastatic carcinoma
Metastatic carcinoma to the adrenal glands can cause primary adrenal insufficiency, typically from lung, breast, kidney, or melanoma primaries. However, metastatic disease would be expected to show discrete adrenal masses on imaging rather than the miliary pulmonary pattern seen here. Additionally, the positive AFB smear and constitutional symptoms over 3 months are more consistent with tuberculosis than malignancy in this epidemiologic setting.

pages.question:
A 55-year-old woman presents to her gynecologist with complaints of frequent hot flashes and night sweats that have been interfering with her sleep and daily activities as a graphic designer for the past 6 months. She reports approximately 10-15 episodes per day, often accompanied by profuse sweating and palpitations. Her medical history is significant for a total hysterectomy 7 years ago due to severe endometriosis, with preservation of both ovaries. She has no history of breast cancer, thromboembolism, or cardiovascular disease. Physical examination reveals a BMI of 24 kg/m² and mild vaginal mucosal thinning. Laboratory evaluation confirms menopause with the values below. She inquires about treatment options to alleviate her symptoms. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial therapy?



Hemoglobin	13.2 g/dL
Hematocrit	39.5%
Red Blood Cell Count	4.4 million/μL
White Blood Cell Count	7.100 /μL
Neutrophils	60%
Lymphocytes	30%
Monocytes	6%
Eosinophils	3%
Basophils	1%
Platelet Count	270.000 /μL
Follicle-Stimulating Hormone (FSH)	38 mIU/mL
Luteinizing Hormone (LH)	12 mIU/mL
Estradiol	25 pg/mL
Thyroid-Stimulating Hormone (TSH)	2.0 mU/L
Prolactin	10 ng/mL
pages.explanation:
Explanation
This menopausal patient has moderate to severe vasomotor symptoms including hot flashes and night sweats, along with mild vaginal atrophy. Laboratory findings confirm menopause (elevated FSH, low estradiol). Due to her prior hysterectomy without a uterus, she is a candidate for estrogen-only menopausal hormone therapy, such as a transdermal estrogen patch, which is first-line for symptom relief. Estrogen-progestin combinations are indicated only for patients with an intact uterus to prevent endometrial hyperplasia. Nonhormonal therapies like SSRIs or gabapentin are second-line options for those with contraindications to hormones or when hormone therapy is declined.
(Choice A)
Paroxetine
While this SSRI is an effective nonhormonal option for vasomotor symptoms, it is considered second-line therapy. Hormone therapy is first-line for patients without contraindications, as it provides superior symptom relief for moderate to severe hot flashes.
(Choice B)
Gabapentin
While gabapentin can effectively reduce hot flashes through its effect on thermoregulatory centers, it is a second-line nonhormonal alternative. For patients eligible for hormone therapy without contraindications, estrogen therapy provides superior symptom relief.
(Choice C)
Oral estrogen-progestin combination
This is incorrect because progestin is not required in patients without a uterus since there is no endometrium to protect. Adding unnecessary progestin may increase risks such as breast cancer, cardiovascular events, and venous thromboembolism without providing additional benefit.
(Choice D)
Transdermal estrogen patch
This is the most appropriate initial therapy as it provides systemic estrogen replacement without the need for progestin in a patient without a uterus, effectively alleviating moderate to severe vasomotor symptoms.
(Choice E)
Vaginal estrogen cream
This provides local relief for vaginal atrophy but does not address systemic vasomotor symptoms like hot flashes and night sweats.

pages.question:
A 28-year-old woman with a history of systemic lupus erythematosus presents with progressive fatigue, dyspnea on exertion, and dark urine for the past three weeks. She denies gastrointestinal bleeding, heavy menstrual periods, or recent infections. Physical examination reveals pallor, mild scleral icterus, and splenomegaly. Laboratory studies are shown below. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's anemia?
Hemoglobin	7.8 g/dL
Hematocrit	23%
Red Blood Cell Count	2.5 million/mm3
White Blood Cell Count	9800/mm3
Platelet Count	240000/mm3
Reticulocyte Count	11%
Sodium	138 mEq/L
Potassium	4.3 mEq/L
Chloride	103 mEq/L
Carbon Dioxide	22 mEq/L
Blood Urea Nitrogen	14 mg/dL
Creatinine	0.8 mg/dL
Glucose	96 mg/dL
Calcium	9.3 mg/dL
AST	29 U/L
ALT	25 U/L
Alkaline Phosphatase	88 U/L
Total Bilirubin	3.1 mg/dL	(range: 0.1–1.2 mg/dL)
Direct Bilirubin	0.3 mg/dL	(range: 0.0-0.3 mg/dL)
Indirect Bilirubin	2.8 mg/dL	(range: 0.2–0.9 mg/dL)
Lactate Dehydrogenase	450 U/L	(range:	140–280 U/L)
Haptoglobin	<10 mg/dL	(range:	30–200 mg/dL)
Direct Antiglobulin Test	IgG positive
Peripheral Smear	Spherocytes and polychromatophilic erythrocytes present
pages.explanation:
Explanation
The patient has anemia with a markedly elevated reticulocyte count, indicating that the bone marrow is responding appropriately by increasing erythrocyte production. This makes causes associated with impaired production (e.g., bone marrow infiltration, nutrient deficiencies, or anemia of chronic inflammation) less likely, as they typically feature low reticulocyte counts. The positive direct antiglobulin test, low haptoglobin, elevated LDH, indirect hyperbilirubinemia, and clinical features are consistent with immune-mediated hemolysis, which can occur as an autoimmune complication in systemic lupus erythematosus.
(Choice A)
Parvovirus B19 infection
Parvovirus B19 specifically infects erythroid precursors in the bone marrow, causing transient aplastic crisis characterized by a very low reticulocyte count (<1%). The markedly elevated reticulocytes (11%) exclude this diagnosis.
(Choice B)
Anemia of chronic disease
Anemia of chronic disease involves cytokine-mediated suppression of erythropoiesis and iron utilization, leading to a characteristically low reticulocyte count. The markedly elevated reticulocytes (11%) and evidence of hemolysis exclude this diagnosis.
(Choice C)
Bone marrow failure or infiltration
Bone marrow infiltration or failure typically impairs erythrocyte production, leading to a low reticulocyte count and inadequate bone marrow response to anemia, which is inconsistent with the markedly elevated reticulocytes (11%) seen here.
(Choice D)
Folate deficiency
Folate deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia with impaired DNA synthesis and erythrocyte production, resulting in a low reticulocyte count despite severe anemia. The markedly elevated reticulocytes (11%) exclude this diagnosis.
(Choice E)
Immune-mediated hemolysis
The elevated reticulocyte count indicates compensatory production in response to erythrocyte destruction, and the positive direct antiglobulin test with clinical features support immune-mediated hemolysis as the cause.

pages.question: A 28-year-old nonsmoking man presents with a 3-month history of intermittent hemoptysis, persistent cough, and episodes of shortness of breath with wheezing localized to the left chest. He has no history of tobacco use, occupational exposures, or recent travel. Physical examination reveals decreased breath sounds over the left lower lung field. Chest x-ray is shown below. CT scan with contrast demonstrates a well-circumscribed, avidly enhancing mass with an endobronchial component obstructing the left main bronchus. Bronchoscopy confirms a polypoid lesion. What is the most likely diagnosis?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
Bronchial carcinoid tumor is a neuroendocrine malignancy arising from bronchial Kulchitsky cells, typically manifesting with bronchial obstruction symptoms (dyspnea, wheezing, cough), hemoptysis, and a contrast-enhancing proximal airway mass with an endobronchial component. This tumor usually occurs in young nonsmokers. Other diagnoses have less typical features and risk factors.
(Choice A)
Primary squamous cell lung carcinoma
Squamous cell carcinoma is typically associated with smoking and older age, and it less commonly presents as a hypervascular endobronchial mass in young patients.
(Choice B)
Bronchial carcinoid tumor
This is the correct diagnosis, as bronchial carcinoid tumors are the most common primary lung malignancy in young nonsmokers, often presenting with hemoptysis, obstructive symptoms, and a hypervascular endobronchial mass on contrast-enhanced CT.
(Choice C)
Metastatic renal cell carcinoma
While metastatic renal cell carcinoma can present as hypervascular pulmonary lesions, it would be extremely uncommon in a young patient without known primary renal malignancy. Primary bronchial carcinoid tumor is far more likely given the patient demographics and endobronchial location.
(Choice D)
Endobronchial hamartoma
Endobronchial hamartomas are benign lesions composed of normal lung tissue elements (cartilage, fat, smooth muscle) that rarely cause hemoptysis and typically do not show avid contrast enhancement on CT imaging, unlike the hypervascular appearance described.

pages.question: A 70-year-old patient visits the clinic with a complaint of severe localized tingling and burning sensation extending across the left side of their chest, which began three days ago. They have a history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) but no recent respiratory symptoms. There are no changes reported in bowel habits, and the patient has had no recent fevers. Vital signs are normal, and a detailed physical exam reveals no rashes initially but significant hypersensitivity on light touch over a single rib section. You predict that in a week, the patient is most likely to develop:
pages.explanation:
Explanation
The symptoms described—localized, burning, and tingling pain over a dermatomal area—are classic for initial manifestations of shingles. The expected progression involves the development of a vesicular rash that aligns with the nerves in the affected dermatome. Immune suppression, as seen in COPD patients using systemic steroids, can predispose to this condition.
(Choice A)
Severe headaches
Headaches are not associated with unilateral chest pain following a dermatomal distribution. The patient's symptoms are localized to a thoracic dermatome, not consistent with cephalic pain patterns.
(Choice B)
Chest wall vesicular rash
The described pain and localized hypersensitivity are suggestive of shingles, where a vesicular rash can develop along a dermatome.
(Choice C)
Tachycardia
While tachycardia can occur with severe pain, it is not a specific sequela of herpes zoster. The question asks what will most likely develop, and the characteristic progression is from prodromal pain to vesicular eruption.
(Choice D)
Radicular arm pain with weakness
While neuropathic pain may manifest in the arm, it does not likely follow after the presentation described, especially without relevant preceding symptoms.
(Choice E)
Purulent chest wall abscess
Purulent discharge suggests bacterial infection or abscess formation, which would typically present with fever, erythema, and warmth. The prodromal burning pain in a dermatomal pattern without systemic signs is characteristic of viral reactivation, not bacterial infection.

pages.question: A 3-week-old male infant is brought to the pediatrician by his parents because of persistent vomiting and poor weight gain since birth. The infant was born at term via uncomplicated vaginal delivery. He has been exclusively breastfed but has had profuse, non-bilious vomiting with each feeding. Physical examination reveals a lethargic infant in the 5th percentile for weight. A urine organic acid panel and plasma amino acid profile are sent. Results show markedly elevated plasma phenylalanine levels with a low tyrosine-to-phenylalanine ratio. Newborn screening had flagged an abnormality but the family had not followed up. The diagnosis of phenylketonuria (PKU) is confirmed. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in nutritional management?

answers.text:
Switch to a standard cow's milk-based infant formula to provide complete nutrition
(0%)

Prescribe a low-phenylalanine pharmaceutical drug as the sole treatment
(0%)

Begin a hydrolyzed protein formula to reduce protein allergenicity
(0%)

Initiate a phenylalanine-free amino acid-based medical food formula as the primary protein source
(100%)

Recommend a dietary supplement containing branched-chain amino acids to support protein synthesis
(0%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
Phenylketonuria requires lifelong dietary phenylalanine restriction, achieved through an amino acid-based medical food that provides all essential amino acids except phenylalanine. These products are regulated by the FDA as medical foods — distinct from dietary supplements — and are intended for use under medical supervision for a condition with distinctive nutritional needs established by recognized medical evaluation. Natural protein intake is severely limited, and the medical food formula serves as the primary protein source.
(Choice A)
Switch to a standard cow's milk-based infant formula to provide complete nutrition
Standard cow's milk-based formulas contain high levels of phenylalanine as part of intact protein and would worsen hyperphenylalaninemia in PKU patients. These formulas provide 2-3 times more phenylalanine per serving than a PKU patient can tolerate. The fundamental principle of PKU management is strict phenylalanine restriction while meeting all other nutritional needs through specialized medical foods.
(Choice B)
Prescribe a low-phenylalanine pharmaceutical drug as the sole treatment
Sapropterin (Kuvan) is a synthetic cofactor (tetrahydrobiopterin) that can enhance residual phenylalanine hydroxylase enzyme activity in some PKU patients, potentially allowing for liberalized dietary phenylalanine intake. However, only 20-50% of PKU patients respond to sapropterin, response varies significantly, and even responders still require dietary phenylalanine restriction. It serves as an adjunct to, not replacement for, phenylalanine-restricted medical foods.
(Choice C)
Begin a hydrolyzed protein formula to reduce protein allergenicity
Hydrolyzed protein formulas are designed to reduce cow's milk protein allergenicity by breaking proteins into smaller peptides, making them useful for food protein allergies or cow's milk protein intolerance. However, these formulas still contain significant amounts of phenylalanine within the hydrolyzed peptides and amino acids, making them inappropriate for PKU management where strict phenylalanine restriction is essential.
(Choice D)
Initiate a phenylalanine-free amino acid-based medical food formula as the primary protein source
Phenylketonuria results from deficiency of phenylalanine hydroxylase, the enzyme that converts phenylalanine to tyrosine, leading to toxic accumulation of phenylalanine which causes irreversible neurocognitive damage if untreated. Management requires severe restriction of dietary phenylalanine, which means natural protein intake must be drastically limited. Phenylalanine-free amino acid-based medical food formulas supply all essential amino acids except phenylalanine, along with vitamins, minerals, and energy, serving as the cornerstone of nutritional therapy. These products are classified as medical foods under the FDA Orphan Drug Act and the 1988 Orphan Drug Amendments, distinct from dietary supplements because they are formulated to meet distinctive nutritional requirements of a specific disease and are intended to be used under medical supervision. Early initiation — ideally within the first days to weeks of life — is critical to prevent neurotoxicity. Small, carefully titrated amounts of natural protein are also provided to supply the minimum phenylalanine needed for normal protein synthesis. Tyrosine supplementation is also often needed because it becomes conditionally essential in PKU.
(Choice E)
Recommend a dietary supplement containing branched-chain amino acids to support protein synthesis
Branched-chain amino acid supplements are used in the management of maple syrup urine disease, not PKU. In PKU, the metabolic defect involves phenylalanine, not the branched-chain amino acids leucine, isoleucine, and valine. Administering a generic amino acid supplement without specifically excluding phenylalanine would not address the underlying metabolic problem and could worsen outcomes.

pages.question: A 67-year-old man with newly diagnosed stage III non-small cell lung cancer presents to his oncologist for an initial treatment planning visit. He has lost 12 pounds over the past 2 months and reports decreased appetite. His BMI is 21 kg/m². The oncology team is planning to initiate platinum-based chemotherapy within the next 2 weeks. He denies any specific food allergies or dietary restrictions. His social history reveals that he lives alone and relies on a fixed income. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in systematically integrating nutrition support into this patient's care?

answers.text:
Order parenteral nutrition immediately given the degree of weight loss and imminent chemotherapy initiation.
(0%)

Refer the patient to a social worker but defer nutrition assessment until after the first chemotherapy cycle is completed.
(0%)

Place a standing dietitian referral order as part of the oncology intake workflow and document food insecurity as an active problem in the medical record.
(100%)

Advise the patient to increase his caloric intake and reassess weight at his next chemotherapy appointment.
(0%)

Prescribe a commercial oral nutritional supplement and document it in the medication reconciliation list without further dietitian involvement.
(0%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
High-risk oncology patients should have standing dietitian referral orders placed at the time of cancer diagnosis and treatment initiation, as malnutrition significantly worsens chemotherapy tolerance and outcomes. Systematic integration of nutrition workflows includes food insecurity screening and documentation as an active problem to trigger appropriate social services coordination. Team-based care models ensure comprehensive nutrition management without relying on individual provider recall or initiative.
(Choice A)
Order parenteral nutrition immediately given the degree of weight loss and imminent chemotherapy initiation.
Parenteral nutrition is not indicated at this stage; the patient has no evidence of a non-functional gastrointestinal tract, and oral or enteral nutrition should always be preferred when feasible. Initiating parenteral nutrition prematurely carries risks of infection, metabolic complications, and cost without demonstrating superiority over enteral approaches in patients who can eat. The first step is structured assessment and dietitian involvement, not invasive nutritional intervention.
(Choice B)
Refer the patient to a social worker but defer nutrition assessment until after the first chemotherapy cycle is completed.
While social worker referral appropriately addresses food insecurity, deferring nutrition assessment until after chemotherapy initiation is problematic. Malnutrition at chemotherapy start independently worsens treatment tolerance, increases toxicity risk, and may delay or interrupt treatment. The optimal approach requires parallel nutrition assessment and social services coordination before treatment begins.
(Choice C)
Place a standing dietitian referral order as part of the oncology intake workflow and document food insecurity as an active problem in the medical record.
Patients with cancer, particularly those initiating chemotherapy, are at high risk for malnutrition and its associated complications, including treatment delays, increased toxicity, and worse survival outcomes. Standing dietitian referral orders for high-risk diagnoses such as cancer are a best-practice strategy for systematically integrating nutrition care without relying on ad hoc clinician action. This patient also exhibits a social vulnerability — fixed income and living alone — that raises concern for food insecurity, which should be documented as an active problem in the medical record to trigger appropriate community resource referrals. Team-based care models distribute nutrition responsibilities across oncologists, nurses, social workers, and registered dietitians, ensuring comprehensive management. Documenting food insecurity as a problem list item also enables tracking, follow-up, and coordination with social services. This approach reflects both clinical nutrition guidelines (ASPEN, ESPEN) and health equity frameworks that recognize food access as a social determinant of health. Early dietitian involvement has been shown to improve quality of life and chemotherapy completion rates in cancer patients.
(Choice D)
Advise the patient to increase his caloric intake and reassess weight at his next chemotherapy appointment.
Advising caloric increases without structured support is insufficient for a patient with significant weight loss (12 pounds in 2 months) who is about to start chemotherapy. Generic dietary advice fails to address this patient's specific nutritional vulnerabilities, food insecurity concerns, and the systematic approach needed for high-risk oncology patients. Deferring formal reassessment misses the critical window for nutrition optimization before treatment.
(Choice E)
Prescribe a commercial oral nutritional supplement and document it in the medication reconciliation list without further dietitian involvement.
Prescribing supplements without comprehensive dietitian assessment represents a fragmented approach that fails to address the patient's complex nutritional needs. This patient requires individualized assessment of his weight loss, food insecurity, and chemotherapy-related nutritional risks. Additionally, this approach completely ignores the systematic workflow integration that ensures consistent nutrition care for all high-risk patients.

pages.question:
A 3-year-old girl with a history of sickle cell disease (HbSS) is brought to the emergency department after a family trip to a high-altitude area. Her parents report that she became increasingly lethargic and complained of upper abdominal discomfort during the travel. On examination, she appears pale and tachypneic, with a heart rate of 150 bpm, blood pressure of 75/45 mm Hg, and a tender spleen palpable 5 cm below the left costal margin. Laboratory results are shown below. After initial intravenous fluid resuscitation with normal saline, the patient's blood pressure improves slightly to 85/50 mm Hg, but she remains tachycardic and lethargic. What is the most appropriate next step in management?



Hemoglobin	6.8 g/dL
Hematocrit	21%
Red Blood Cell Count	2.1 million/mm3
White Blood Cell Count	14000/μL
Neutrophils	72%
Lymphocytes	20%
Monocytes	6%
Eosinophils	1%
Basophils	1%
Platelet Count	250000/μL
Reticulocyte Count	12%	(range: 0.5–2.5%)
pages.explanation:
Explanation
This patient is experiencing an acute splenic sequestration crisis, a life-threatening complication of sickle cell disease where red blood cells become trapped in the enlarged spleen, leading to rapid onset of severe anemia, splenomegaly, and hypovolemic shock. The high-altitude exposure likely triggered sickling and vaso-occlusion. After initial fluid resuscitation to address hypovolemia, packed red blood cell transfusion is essential to correct the severe anemia and restore oxygen-carrying capacity. Careful monitoring is required to avoid fluid overload, and parents should be counseled about avoiding high-altitude travel in the future.
(Choice A)
Broad-spectrum antibiotics
While infections can trigger sickle cell crises, this patient's presentation is classic for splenic sequestration (high-altitude trigger, splenomegaly, severe anemia) without fever or other signs of infection. The elevated white blood cell count is likely due to stress/pain rather than infection. Antibiotics would not address the primary pathophysiology of red blood cell trapping in the spleen.
(Choice B)
Exchange transfusion
Exchange transfusion involves removing the patient's sickle cells while simultaneously replacing them with normal red blood cells. It is reserved for severe complications like acute chest syndrome, stroke, or multiorgan failure where rapid reduction of sickle cell percentage is critical. Simple transfusion is sufficient for isolated splenic sequestration crisis to restore circulating red blood cell mass.
(Choice C)
Packed red blood cell transfusion
This is the correct next step. The patient has severe anemia due to splenic sequestration, and transfusion of packed red blood cells is necessary to restore oxygen-carrying capacity after initial fluid resuscitation.
(Choice D)
Hydroxyurea administration
Hydroxyurea is a disease-modifying therapy used for long-term management of sickle cell disease to increase fetal hemoglobin levels and reduce crisis frequency. It has no role in acute management of splenic sequestration crisis, as it takes weeks to months to show clinical benefit and does not address the immediate life-threatening anemia.
(Choice E)
Emergency splenectomy
Emergency splenectomy is not indicated for acute splenic sequestration crisis. While splenectomy may be considered for prevention of recurrent sequestration episodes (typically after 2 or more episodes), the immediate priority is correcting the severe anemia and hypovolemia with transfusion. Emergency surgery would be inappropriate and dangerous in this hemodynamically unstable patient.

pages.question: A 48-year-old man with hyperlipidemia presents for dietary counseling. His LDL is 178 mg/dL and he has declined statin therapy. During the visit his physician uses a motivational interviewing technique and asks: "On a scale of 0 to 10, how important is it to you to make changes to your diet to lower your cholesterol, and on a scale of 0 to 10, how confident are you that you could make those changes if you decided to?" The patient responds: "Importance is probably a 7 — I definitely don't want a heart attack. But confidence is maybe a 3 — I travel constantly for work and eat out at restaurants almost every day, so I don't see how I could really control what I eat." Which of the following represents the most appropriate motivational interviewing response to this patient's ruler scores?

answers.text:
Address the low importance score first by providing additional education about cardiovascular risks of untreated hyperlipidemia to increase his motivation before discussing practical solutions
(0%)

Inform the patient that a confidence score of 3 indicates he is not yet ready for dietary change and recommend starting statin therapy instead of pursuing dietary modification
(0%)

Acknowledge the high importance score, focus counseling on building confidence by exploring what small changes might be achievable within his travel and restaurant constraints, and ask what would need to be different to raise his confidence score from a 3 to a 4 or 5
(100%)

Interpret both scores as indicating insufficient motivation and defer dietary counseling to a future visit when the patient expresses greater readiness
(0%)

Develop a detailed meal plan focused on home cooking and recommend requesting hotel rooms with kitchenettes to enable self-preparation of heart-healthy meals during business travel
(0%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
This patient has high importance (7/10) but low confidence (3/10) — a pattern indicating that the primary barrier to dietary change is not motivation but self-efficacy. The appropriate MI response explores what would need to be different to raise his confidence, identifies small achievable changes within his current constraints (restaurant eating strategies), and uses the importance score to elicit change talk rather than addressing importance, which is already adequate.
(Choice A)
Address the low importance score first by providing additional education about cardiovascular risks of untreated hyperlipidemia to increase his motivation before discussing practical solutions
This response incorrectly identifies the patient's importance score of 7/10 as 'low' when it actually indicates high motivation for dietary change. The patient explicitly states he doesn't want a heart attack, demonstrating he already understands the importance of cholesterol management. Providing cardiovascular risk education to someone who already rates importance at 7/10 would be redundant and potentially condescending, while ignoring the actual barrier identified by his low confidence score (3/10). Effective motivational interviewing responds to what the patient's scores reveal rather than following a generic counseling script.
(Choice B)
Inform the patient that a confidence score of 3 indicates he is not yet ready for dietary change and recommend starting statin therapy instead of pursuing dietary modification
This response incorrectly interprets a confidence score of 3/10 as grounds for abandoning dietary counseling entirely. In motivational interviewing, low confidence scores identify specific self-efficacy gaps that become the focus of therapeutic intervention, not reasons to abandon the patient's preferred approach. The patient has already declined statin therapy and expressed preference for dietary modification. Rather than respecting patient autonomy and working to build confidence within his constraints, this approach dismisses his preferences and imposes an unwanted pharmacological solution.
(Choice C)
Acknowledge the high importance score, focus counseling on building confidence by exploring what small changes might be achievable within his travel and restaurant constraints, and ask what would need to be different to raise his confidence score from a 3 to a 4 or 5
The importance-confidence ruler (also called the readiness ruler) is a core motivational interviewing assessment tool that simultaneously evaluates two distinct dimensions of motivation: importance (how much the patient values the change — the "why") and confidence (the patient's belief in their ability to successfully make the change — self-efficacy, the "how"). This patient's divergent scores reveal the specific barrier to dietary change: he values cholesterol management highly (7/10) but does not believe he can implement change given his lifestyle constraints (3/10). Responding to high importance scores: Because his importance score is already 7/10, spending counseling time on why dietary change matters would be redundant and potentially condescending. Instead, the physician can briefly affirm: "It sounds like this really does matter to you — a 7 is significant." Using the importance to elicit change talk: "You said a 7 — what makes it that high rather than lower?" invites the patient to articulate his own reasons for change, which are more persuasive than physician-generated reasons. Responding to low confidence scores: The critical therapeutic work is confidence-building. The MI technique of asking "What would need to be different to move from a 3 to a 4?" invites problem-solving without the physician imposing solutions. In this patient's case, the barrier is specific and concrete — restaurant eating during frequent travel. Exploring what is achievable within this constraint might reveal: ordering grilled rather than fried proteins; choosing vegetable-based sides; requesting dressings on the side; selecting fish or plant-based entrees from restaurant menus; avoiding processed appetizers and bread baskets. These are achievable dietary modifications that require no home cooking and respect the patient's actual life circumstances. Building confidence through small achievable success: identifying one restaurant-compatible dietary change he feels a 6–7/10 confident about implementing produces early success that builds self-efficacy for subsequent changes.
(Choice D)
Interpret both scores as indicating insufficient motivation and defer dietary counseling to a future visit when the patient expresses greater readiness
This response misinterprets the ruler scores entirely. An importance score of 7/10 indicates substantial motivation for change, while a confidence score of 3/10 identifies a specific self-efficacy barrier rather than insufficient overall readiness. Deferring counseling based on low confidence scores contradicts motivational interviewing principles - low confidence represents the therapeutic target, not a contraindication to counseling. This approach wastes the opportunity to address the patient's clearly identified and potentially solvable barrier (restaurant eating during travel).
(Choice E)
Develop a detailed meal plan focused on home cooking and recommend requesting hotel rooms with kitchenettes to enable self-preparation of heart-healthy meals during business travel
Prescribing a home cooking-based meal plan to a patient who has explicitly identified constant restaurant eating as his primary barrier is a stage-mismatched and context-ignorant intervention. This response fails to hear the patient's specific constraint and imposes a solution that is impractical given his stated circumstances. An MI-consistent approach works within the patient's actual life context — restaurant eating during travel — rather than prescribing an idealized lifestyle that requires him to restructure his professional life.

pages.question: A 62-year-old woman with a body mass index of 35 kg/m² and a history of endometrial cancer treated with hysterectomy 6 months ago presents to the emergency department with acute onset of shortness of breath, wheezing, and right-sided chest pain. She reports recent long-distance travel by car. On examination, she is tachypneic with oxygen saturation of 92% on room air, and auscultation reveals wheezing in the right lung field. There is mild swelling in her left calf. Electrocardiogram is shown below. Which of the following is the most likely finding on arterial blood gas analysis in this patient?

answers.text:
Decreased partial pressure of carbon dioxide with acidosis
(5.41%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
This patient's risk factors (obesity, malignancy, immobility from travel) and presentation (acute dyspnea, wheezing, hypoxia, leg swelling) suggest pulmonary embolism from deep venous thrombosis. The hallmark physiological abnormality is ventilation-perfusion mismatch leading to an elevated alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient on arterial blood gas analysis.
(Choice A)
Metabolic alkalosis
Metabolic alkalosis is not typical in acute PE; it might occur in other conditions like vomiting or diuretic use.
(Choice B)
Decreased partial pressure of carbon dioxide with acidosis
This describes metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation (Kussmaul breathing). In acute PE, patients typically develop respiratory alkalosis due to tachypnea and hyperventilation in response to hypoxia, resulting in low pCO2 with alkalosis, not acidosis.
(Choice C)
Normal alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient
A normal A-a gradient would suggest either hypoventilation or low inspired oxygen as the cause of hypoxia. In PE, the ventilation-perfusion mismatch creates dead space ventilation (ventilated but not perfused areas), which characteristically elevates the A-a gradient.
(Choice D)
Elevated alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient
Pulmonary embolism causes ventilation-perfusion mismatch, which increases the alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient, leading to hypoxia despite adequate ventilation.
(Choice E)
Respiratory acidosis with hypercapnia
PE typically causes tachypnea and hyperventilation as a compensatory response to hypoxia and increased dead space ventilation. This leads to respiratory alkalosis with hypocapnia, not respiratory acidosis with hypercapnia which would suggest hypoventilation.

pages.question: A 28-year-old female professional ballet dancer with a history of type 1 diabetes mellitus presents with a non-healing ulcer on the plantar surface of her right great toe. She reports wearing tight pointe shoes for several hours daily and notes that the ulcer is painless despite ongoing activity. Physical examination reveals a 2 cm punched-out ulcer with hyperkeratotic borders, no erythema, and no purulent drainage. Sensory testing demonstrates decreased light touch and vibration sensation in both feet, with normal pedal pulses. Which of the following diagnostic tests is most likely to identify the underlying cause of this patient's ulcer?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
The patient has a painless, punched-out ulcer on the plantar surface of the great toe with risk factors including type 1 diabetes and peripheral neuropathy from repeated pressure in pointe shoes. The explanation focuses on the diagnosis of neuropathic (diabetic) foot ulcers and why each diagnostic choice is likely or unlikely. Ankle-brachial index measures arterial disease, wound culture identifies potential infection but not etiology, venous duplex ultrasound assesses for venous insufficiency, lumbosacral MRI evaluates for radiculopathy, erythrocyte sedimentation rate screens for inflammatory or infectious processes, which are less consistent with this presentation.
(Choice A)
Venous duplex ultrasound
This evaluates for venous insufficiency, which causes ulcers usually on the medial ankle with associated edema and skin changes, not matching this painless, punched-out ulcer on a weight-bearing site.
(Choice B)
Lumbosacral MRI
Lumbosacral MRI evaluates for structural causes of neuropathy such as radiculopathy or spinal stenosis. However, in a patient with established type 1 diabetes presenting with classic signs of peripheral neuropathy (decreased sensation in stocking distribution), diabetic neuropathy is the most likely cause and does not require spinal imaging.
(Choice C)
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate
This nonspecific marker of inflammation could indicate infection or vasculitis, but the ulcer shows no signs of infection, and the clinical picture fits neuropathic etiology without systemic inflammation.
(Choice D)
Hemoglobin A1c assay
This test evaluates long-term glycemic control, which is critical in the pathogenesis of diabetic peripheral neuropathy leading to loss of protective sensation and subsequent ulcer formation from repeated trauma.
(Choice E)
Deep tissue wound culture
A wound culture may identify bacterial colonization or infection, which could complicate the ulcer but does not address the underlying etiology of insensate skin leading to trauma.

pages.question: A 35-year-old woman, gravida 1, at 28 weeks' gestation presents to her obstetrician with complaints of increased shortness of breath, wheezing, and nighttime awakenings due to coughing over the past month. She has a history of mild persistent asthma diagnosed in adolescence, which has been well controlled for the last 5 years on a daily inhaled corticosteroid and as-needed short-acting beta-agonist. She reports no recent infections, changes in environment, or new allergens, but mentions she has been under stress due to work demands as a librarian. Her vital signs are normal, and physical examination reveals mild expiratory wheezing. Spirometry shows a forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1) of 75% predicted, down from 90% at her last visit 6 months ago. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial response by the physician?

answers.text:
"It seems like your asthma is worsening due to pregnancy changes; we should switch to oral medications since inhalers may not be safe for the baby."
(4.62%)

"Your symptoms are likely stress-related from work; I recommend reducing work hours and temporarily stopping your inhalers until after delivery to avoid any medication risks."
(0%)

"Your asthma control has worsened; can you walk me through how and when you use your daily inhaler?"
(83.08%)

"Pregnancy can exacerbate asthma; let's increase your corticosteroid dose immediately to prevent complications."
(12.31%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
In a pregnant patient with longstanding well-controlled asthma presenting with worsening symptoms, nonadherence to controller medications due to fears of fetal harm is a common issue. Most asthma medications are safe in pregnancy and should be continued. The initial approach should involve a nonjudgmental discussion about medication usage patterns to identify and address potential nonadherence.
(Choice A)
"It seems like your asthma is worsening due to pregnancy changes; we should switch to oral medications since inhalers may not be safe for the baby."
This is incorrect because it perpetuates the dangerous misconception that inhaled corticosteroids and bronchodilators are unsafe in pregnancy. In fact, most inhaled asthma medications (including inhaled corticosteroids and short-acting beta-agonists) are safe and preferred over oral medications in pregnancy. Uncontrolled asthma poses far greater risks to both mother and fetus than properly used inhaled medications.
(Choice B)
"Your symptoms are likely stress-related from work; I recommend reducing work hours and temporarily stopping your inhalers until after delivery to avoid any medication risks."
This is incorrect because it attributes worsening asthma solely to psychological stress without investigating the more likely cause of medication nonadherence. Additionally, discontinuing controller medications would be dangerous and could lead to severe asthma exacerbations that pose significant risks to both mother and fetus. Stress may contribute to asthma symptoms but should not be the primary focus without first ensuring proper medication use.
(Choice C)
"Your asthma control has worsened; can you walk me through how and when you use your daily inhaler?"
This is correct as it initiates a nonjudgmental inquiry into medication adherence, which is likely the cause given the history of good control, and reinforces that medications should be continued.
(Choice D)
"Pregnancy can exacerbate asthma; let's increase your corticosteroid dose immediately to prevent complications."
This is incorrect because it assumes pregnancy is directly causing asthma worsening and jumps immediately to medication intensification without first assessing current medication adherence. While pregnancy can affect asthma control (with roughly equal proportions of patients experiencing improvement, worsening, or no change), the most common cause of deteriorating control in previously well-controlled patients is medication nonadherence. Proper assessment of current medication use should precede any dose adjustments.

pages.question: A 28-year-old landscaper presents to the emergency department after a string trimmer malfunctioned, propelling a small piece of debris at high speed into his left eye. He complains of intense pain, photophobia, and markedly reduced vision in the affected eye. Initial examination reveals visual acuity of counting fingers at 1 meter, intraocular pressure of 9 mmHg, and a sluggish pupillary response. Which of the following findings on slit-lamp examination would most strongly indicate an open globe laceration?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
This patient sustained a high-velocity projectile injury from landscaping equipment, raising suspicion for open globe laceration (OGL). Key signs include a teardrop-shaped pupil, decreased visual acuity, and low intraocular pressure. Immediate management involves eye shielding and emergent ophthalmology consultation.
(Choice A)
Teardrop-shaped pupil
A teardrop or peaked pupil is a classic sign of open globe laceration due to iris prolapse through a corneal or scleral wound, pulling the pupil into an irregular shape.
(Choice B)
Elevated intraocular pressure
Open globe laceration characteristically causes reduced intraocular pressure (hypotony) due to leakage of aqueous humor through the wound. Elevated IOP would be inconsistent with an open globe and might suggest other conditions like traumatic hyphema or angle-closure.
(Choice C)
Clear vitreous without hemorrhage
In open globe laceration, vitreous hemorrhage or extrusion is common; a clear vitreous would be atypical and suggest a less penetrating injury.
(Choice D)
Normal afferent pupillary response
A relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) is commonly present in open globe laceration due to retinal detachment, vitreous hemorrhage, or optic nerve injury. A normal pupillary response would be inconsistent with the severity of injury suggested by the clinical presentation.
(Choice E)
Symmetric anterior chamber depth
A symmetric anterior chamber depth would not suggest open globe laceration. In open globe injury, the affected eye typically shows a shallow or flat anterior chamber compared to the unaffected eye due to aqueous humor leakage through the wound.

pages.question: In a study designed to evaluate the effectiveness of a novel weight loss program, participants start changing their eating habits and exercise routines once they learn they are being observed. What type of phenomenon could be impacting the study results?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
In clinical and behavioral studies, the Hawthorne effect can represent a significant challenge as participants modify their actions simply because they are aware of being enrolled in a study. This effect highlights the importance of designing studies that minimize such biases to accurately assess interventions' efficacy.
(Choice A)
Placebo effect
The placebo effect occurs when participants experience real improvements in symptoms or outcomes due to their psychological belief that they are receiving an effective treatment, regardless of the treatment's actual pharmacological or physiological effects. This is distinct from behavioral changes due to awareness of observation.
(Choice B)
Selection bias
Selection bias occurs when the participants included in a study are not representative of the target population. It does not involve behavioral changes due to awareness but rather issues in how subjects are chosen for the study.
(Choice C)
Hawthorne effect
The Hawthorne effect describes situations where study participants modify their behavior simply because they are being watched, which can jeopardize the validity of study results as seen in interventions affecting behavioral changes.
(Choice D)
Recall bias
Recall bias occurs in studies collecting retrospective data when participants have impaired or inaccurate recall about events, leading to bias. It is not connected to being observed in a study setting.
(Choice E)
Observer bias
Observer bias occurs when researchers' expectations or knowledge of group assignments influence how they collect, interpret, or record data. This involves the investigator's influence on results, not participants changing behavior due to awareness of being observed.

pages.question: A 52-year-old man presents with a 4-month history of progressive pain in the posterior aspect of his right ankle. He reports that the pain started after he began training intensively for a charity walkathon, having previously led a sedentary lifestyle as an accountant. The pain is worse during and after walking, and he notes morning stiffness in the ankle that improves with light activity. On examination, there is tenderness along the Achilles tendon approximately 4 cm proximal to its insertion on the calcaneus, with mild swelling but no ecchymosis or palpable defect. Ankle dorsiflexion elicits pain, but Thompson test is negative. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

answers.text:
Prolonged immobilization in a walking boot
(18.52%)

High-dose oral nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs alone
(18.52%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
This patient most likely has chronic Achilles tendinopathy, presenting with persistent ankle pain and tenderness proximal to the tendon's insertion on the calcaneus following an abrupt increase in physical activity. For chronic symptoms, the recommended management includes a rehabilitation program focusing on eccentric resistance exercises. Activity modification, icing, and NSAIDs are more appropriate for acute phases, while corticosteroid injections and surgical interventions are not indicated for uncomplicated cases.
(Choice A)
Immediate surgical debridement and repair
Surgical intervention is reserved for cases of Achilles tendon rupture or severe, refractory tendinopathy; it is not indicated for uncomplicated chronic Achilles tendinopathy.
(Choice B)
Prolonged immobilization in a walking boot
Prolonged immobilization leads to muscle atrophy, joint stiffness, and tendon deconditioning without addressing the underlying pathophysiology of tendinopathy. Current evidence supports controlled loading through progressive exercises rather than rest for chronic tendinopathy.
(Choice C)
Corticosteroid injection into the tendon
Corticosteroid injections are contraindicated in Achilles tendinopathy due to the significant risk of tendon weakening and rupture. While they may provide short-term pain relief, they impair tendon healing and increase the risk of catastrophic tendon failure.
(Choice D)
Eccentric calf-strengthening exercises
For chronic Achilles tendinopathy, a structured rehabilitation program with eccentric resistance exercises is the evidence-based first-line treatment to promote tendon healing and strength.
(Choice E)
High-dose oral nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs alone
While NSAIDs may provide symptomatic relief for acute pain and inflammation, they do not address the underlying degenerative changes in chronic tendinopathy. Monotherapy with NSAIDs lacks the rehabilitative component necessary for tendon remodeling and long-term recovery.

pages.question:
A 32-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after collapsing at home. She reports heavy vaginal bleeding for the past 24 hours following a recent miscarriage. On examination, she is pale, with a blood pressure of 85/55 mm Hg, heart rate of 130 beats/min, cool and clammy extremities, and flat neck veins. Laboratory studies are shown below. She is suspected to have hypovolemic shock due to postpartum hemorrhage. A bedside echocardiogram is performed to assess her cardiac function. Which of the following echocardiographic findings is most likely in this patient?



White blood cell count	6.8x10^3/µL
Neutrophils	60%
Lymphocytes	30%
Monocytes	7%
Eosinophils	2%
Basophils	1%
Red blood cell count	2.4x10^6/µL
Hemoglobin	7 g/dL
Hematocrit	21%
Mean corpuscular volume	88 fL
Mean corpuscular hemoglobin	29 pg
Mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration	33 g/dL
Red cell distribution width	14.5%
Platelet count	250x10^3/µL
Mean platelet volume	9.5 fL

answers.text:
Pericardial effusion with right atrial collapse
(2.6%)

Dilated left ventricle with reduced ejection fraction of 30%
(12.99%)

Hyperdynamic left ventricle with ejection fraction of 80% and normal cavity size
(45.45%)

Right ventricular dilation with McConnell's sign
(0%)

Small left ventricular cavity volume with ejection fraction of 75%
(38.96%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
The patient's presentation with hypotension, tachycardia, cool extremities, flat neck veins, and history of heavy vaginal bleeding following miscarriage is most consistent with hypovolemic shock due to hemorrhagic blood loss. In hypovolemic shock, echocardiographic findings typically include a small left ventricular cavity volume due to decreased preload, with a compensatory increase in ejection fraction to maintain cardiac output. This differentiates it from cardiogenic shock (dilated ventricle with low ejection fraction), obstructive shock like cardiac tamponade (pericardial effusion with chamber collapse), massive pulmonary embolism (right ventricular dilation and strain), and distributive shock (hyperdynamic function with normal or increased cardiac output but low systemic vascular resistance, often without cold extremities).
(Choice A)
Pericardial effusion with right atrial collapse
This suggests cardiac tamponade, a form of obstructive shock where pericardial fluid compresses the heart and impairs ventricular filling. However, the patient lacks the classic Beck's triad findings (elevated JVP, muffled heart sounds, hypotension with pulsus paradoxus), has flat neck veins indicating low preload rather than impaired filling, and her clinical history clearly points to hemorrhagic rather than pericardial pathology.
(Choice B)
Dilated left ventricle with reduced ejection fraction of 30%
This is characteristic of cardiogenic shock, where pump failure leads to low cardiac output and high filling pressures, but the patient has no signs of heart failure and has flat neck veins indicating low preload.
(Choice C)
Hyperdynamic left ventricle with ejection fraction of 80% and normal cavity size
This hyperdynamic pattern is characteristic of distributive shock (such as sepsis or anaphylaxis), where systemic vascular resistance is severely reduced, leading to compensatory increased cardiac output and warm, vasodilated extremities. However, this patient presents with cold, clammy extremities indicating vasoconstriction (not vasodilation) and has a clear hemorrhagic etiology rather than inflammatory or allergic triggers.
(Choice D)
Right ventricular dilation with McConnell's sign
This is seen in massive pulmonary embolism causing obstructive shock, with right heart strain, but the patient has no risk factors for thromboembolism, respiratory symptoms, or evidence of right heart overload.
(Choice E)
Small left ventricular cavity volume with ejection fraction of 75%
This finding reflects decreased preload and compensatory hypercontractility in hypovolemic shock, which matches the patient's clinical picture of hemorrhagic blood loss.

pages.question:
A 62-year-old female visits the clinic due to frequent urination and excessive thirst over the past three months. She also mentions occasional muscle cramps and constant fatigue throughout the day. She experienced a temporary episode of muscle weakness on one occasion but recovered within several hours. She has been a non-smoker all her life and rarely consumes alcohol. Her overall health history is otherwise uneventful. On examination, her heart rate is 84 beats per minute, and her blood pressure measures 160/100 mmHg. Her temperature is within normal limits. Neurological assessment is unremarkable. Lab results include the following:  
 Plasma sodium: 144 mEq/L  
 Plasma potassium: 2.7 mEq/L  
 Serum creatinine: 0.9 mg/dL  
 Plasma renin activity: low  
 Plasma aldosterone concentration: high  
Which of the following is the most accurate diagnosis?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
In cases where a patient presents with high blood pressure and hypokalemia, primary hyperaldosteronism is often suspected due to its distinct biochemical pattern: suppressed plasma renin activity and increased aldosterone secretion. This hormonal imbalance results in electrolyte disturbances that manifest clinically as hypertension and muscle weakness, among other symptoms.
(Choice A)
Liddle syndrome
Liddle syndrome causes hypertension and hypokalemia through constitutively active epithelial sodium channels, but is characterized by suppressed renin AND aldosterone levels, unlike this patient who has elevated aldosterone.
(Choice B)
Primary hyperaldosteronism
Patients with primary hyperaldosteronism typically exhibit low PRA and elevated aldosterone levels, as seen here.
(Choice C)
Renovascular hypertension
Renovascular hypertension activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, resulting in elevated plasma renin activity and secondary aldosterone elevation. This patient's low renin activity excludes this diagnosis.
(Choice D)
Renin-secreting tumor
A renin-secreting tumor would present with increased PRA, which is not the case here.
(Choice E)
Hypokalemic periodic paralysis
Hypokalemic periodic paralysis presents with episodic muscle weakness triggered by potassium shifts, but patients typically have normal blood pressure and normal renin-aldosterone levels between episodes, unlike this patient's sustained hypertension and hormonal abnormalities.

pages.question: A 28-year-old man with type 1 diabetes mellitus, managed with a basal-bolus insulin regimen, presents for advice on starting a new endurance cycling program. He plans to cycle for 90 minutes, 4 times per week, and is concerned about hypoglycemia during and after sessions. His current regimen includes insulin glargine at bedtime and insulin aspart before meals. He maintains good glycemic control with hemoglobin A1c of 6.8%. What is the most appropriate recommendation to prevent exercise-induced hypoglycemia?

answers.text:
Decrease doses of insulin glargine and insulin aspart
(65.96%)

Increase doses of insulin glargine and insulin aspart
(0%)

Test urine ketones before each cycling session
(1.06%)

Limit cycling sessions to 30 minutes to minimize hypoglycemia risk
(9.57%)

Discontinue insulin glargine during training days
(23.4%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
Exercise increases glucose uptake by skeletal muscle cells through both insulin-dependent and insulin-independent mechanisms. Patients with type 1 diabetes taking basal-bolus insulin should reduce premeal bolus insulin prior to exercise; for prolonged exercise (>60-90 minutes), modest reduction of basal insulin may also be considered. Patients starting strenuous exercise should increase carbohydrate intake, especially for sessions >60 minutes. Additional strategies include checking blood glucose before, during (for sessions >60 minutes), and after exercise. Limiting sessions to 30 minutes, discontinuing basal insulin entirely, routinely testing urine ketones, or increasing insulin doses are not appropriate.
(Choice A)
Decrease doses of insulin glargine and insulin aspart
For patients with type 1 diabetes on basal-bolus insulin, reducing the pre-exercise bolus insulin and, for prolonged exercise, the basal insulin helps prevent hypoglycemia due to increased glucose uptake by muscles.
(Choice B)
Increase doses of insulin glargine and insulin aspart
Increasing insulin doses would heighten the risk of hypoglycemia during exercise, as exercise already enhances insulin-independent glucose uptake.
(Choice C)
Test urine ketones before each cycling session
Routine urine ketone testing before exercise is unnecessary for well-controlled type 1 diabetes patients; ketone monitoring is indicated when blood glucose is elevated (>250 mg/dL) or during illness, not as part of routine exercise preparation.
(Choice D)
Limit cycling sessions to 30 minutes to minimize hypoglycemia risk
Limiting exercise duration is not necessary; appropriate insulin adjustments and carbohydrate intake allow for longer sessions without undue risk.
(Choice E)
Discontinue insulin glargine during training days
Completely discontinuing basal insulin is dangerous and inappropriate as it removes essential background insulin coverage, leading to hyperglycemia and potential diabetic ketoacidosis; modest dose reduction of basal insulin may be considered for very prolonged exercise sessions.

pages.question: A 52-year-old man with a 20-year history of plaque psoriasis presents with a 6-month history of progressive pain and swelling in his hands and feet. He describes morning stiffness lasting approximately 90 minutes that improves with physical activity throughout the day. On physical examination, there is asymmetric tenderness and swelling involving the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints of the second and third fingers on the right hand, the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joints of the left hand, and the DIP joints of the first and second toes bilaterally. His fingernails exhibit extensive pitting and onycholysis. Laboratory evaluation reveals an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, but rheumatoid factor and anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies are negative. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
This patient has asymmetric inflammatory arthritis involving the DIP joints, morning stiffness improving with activity, nail pitting, and a long-standing history of psoriasis, which are highly characteristic of psoriatic arthritis. Psoriatic arthritis affects 15%-30% of patients with psoriasis and often presents with asymmetric oligoarthritis or symmetric polyarthritis, frequently involving DIP joints and associated with nail changes like pitting. The negative rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP antibodies help distinguish it from rheumatoid arthritis. Other options are less consistent with the combination of findings.
(Choice A)
Reactive arthritis
Reactive arthritis follows genitourinary or gastrointestinal infection, often involves lower extremities with enthesitis, and may have skin lesions like keratoderma blennorrhagicum, but not typically nail pitting or long-standing plaque psoriasis.
(Choice B)
Osteoarthritis
Osteoarthritis typically involves DIP joints but is degenerative, not inflammatory, and does not cause prolonged morning stiffness, asymmetric distribution with inflammation, or nail changes like pitting.
(Choice C)
Gout
Gout typically presents as acute monoarticular attacks, most commonly affecting the first metatarsophalangeal joint initially. It is associated with hyperuricemia and tophi in chronic cases, but does not cause nail pitting or the described pattern of chronic symmetric/asymmetric inflammatory polyarthritis.
(Choice D)
Rheumatoid arthritis
Rheumatoid arthritis typically presents with symmetric polyarthritis primarily involving PIP and metacarpophalangeal joints while sparing DIP joints. Most patients (70-80%) have positive rheumatoid factor or anti-CCP antibodies, and nail pitting is not a feature of RA.
(Choice E)
Psoriatic arthritis
Psoriatic arthritis fits with the long-standing psoriasis, asymmetric involvement including DIP joints, nail pitting, inflammatory morning stiffness improving with activity, and negative serologies.
